Classical RSM fits polynomial surface ordinary least squares (OLS) locates optimum computing stationary point analytically. fast interpretable, approach delivers point estimates optimum provides measure uncertainty around . high-stakes expensive experimental settings, drug formulation, semiconductor manufacturing, agricultural field trials, knowing optimum matters less knowing confident location. nominal 95% confidence interval OLS delta method often -covers small samples, classical curvature classification (maximum / minimum / saddle) binary quantify probability stationary point , example, true maximum. brsm package addresses limitations fitting quadratic response surface within fully Bayesian framework using Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) via Stan brms interface. Every posterior draw model coefficients implies draw stationary point, draw Hessian eigenvalues, draw predicted surface. text: Closed-form posterior distributions available model general. brsm therefore uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) implemented Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) via brms interface (Bürkner, 2017). HMC Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) algorithm exploits gradient information log-posterior make large, efficient proposals, achieving much better mixing random-walk Metropolis–Hastings high-dimensional continuous parameter spaces. default sampling configuration uses 4 chains, 2,000 iterations (1,000 warmup), yielding 4,000 post-warmup posterior draws. text: brsm package provides complete Bayesian workflow second-order response surface analysis. key contributions classical RSM : Full uncertainty propagation: uncertainty stationary point, curvature class, ridge path quantified coherently posterior coefficient draws, rather delta-method approximations. Calibrated credible intervals: simulation studies confirm near-nominal 95% coverage across sample sizes noise levels tested, substantially outperforming OLS delta method small nn. Probabilistic curvature classification: posterior probability maximum, minimum, saddle point informative binary decision, remains meaningful even sample sizes small. LACK-OF-FIT TEST lof_test <- loftest_brsm(   object = fit,   reference_type = "cubic",   include_ppc = TRUE )
